description:
Team from Rivne, Ukraine working on "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots". 

We're building a web app that merges 20+ years of MODIS and VIIRS active fire data into a single consistent burning activity calendar, so fire managers and researchers can explore seasonal patterns and anomalies in any area of interest.
summary:
MODIS × VIIRS Harmonized is a web application that brings NASA FIRMS active-fire data from two sensor generations into one picture. MODIS and VIIRS describe the same fire differently: 1 km versus 375 m pixels, confidence as a percentage versus a letter, different brightness channels, and separate near real-time and standard-processing products. That makes it hard to compare or combine them.
 Our pipeline downloads any period and area from the FIRMS API in background jobs, normalizes every record into a single schema with one three-level confidence scale, and keeps the raw values. On top of it, an interactive map shows detections as a global heat grid or as individual points, ranks fire hotspots by severity, and adds filters, a daily activity calendar and history charts that always follow the current map view.
 The result lets responders, researchers and journalists see where fire activity concentrates and how it changes over time, without reconciling the datasets themselves. The site is live at https://modis-viirs-harmonized.duckdns.org.
details:
What it does

MODIS × VIIRS Harmonized is a web application that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire data from two sensor generations into one consistent picture. A user picks a FIRMS product, a period and an area; the system downloads the data in the background, brings it to a single schema and shows it on an interactive map at https://modis-viirs-harmonized.duckdns.org.

How it works

1. Ingest. Background jobs request CSV data from the NASA FIRMS API for eight products: MODIS and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), each in near real-time and standard processing. Responses are validated, bad rows are rejected without losing the batch, and duplicates are skipped.

2. Harmonize. Every record is stored in one table with one UTC timestamp. MODIS confidence (0–100 %) and VIIRS confidence (low, nominal, high) are mapped to one three-level scale: 0–29 is low, 30–79 nominal, 80–100 high. Raw values, pixel size and all brightness channels are kept. Near real-time and standard-processing data are never mixed, so a fire is not counted twice.

3. Explore. Zoomed out, the map shows detections aggregated into grid cells; zoomed in, individual points coloured by sensor, confidence or fire radiative power. Nearby detections are grouped into hotspots and ranked as elevated, high or critical. Filters, a summary bar, a daily activity calendar and history charts always describe the current map view or a searched country, region or city.

Benefits and intended impact

Anyone comparing MODIS and VIIRS today has to reconcile resolution, confidence scales and product types by hand. Our tool does it once, in the pipeline, so responders, researchers, journalists and students can see where fire activity concentrates and how it changes over time, and filter both sensor families with one confidence setting. Because the raw values are preserved and shown next to the harmonized ones, the result stays traceable to the original NASA data.

Tools and technologies

- Data: NASA FIRMS API (MODIS, VIIRS), NASA GIBS daily satellite imagery, Natural Earth place names.

- Backend: Python 3.14, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy (async), Alembic, Celery with Redis, PostgreSQL 17.

- Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Leaflet.

- Infrastructure: Docker Compose on AWS EC2, nginx with HTTPS, Terraform, GitHub Actions CI/CD with automatic deployment.

- Quality: automated test suites for the backend and the frontend run on every change.

What makes it creative

Instead of two separate layers, the two sensor families share one confidence scale and one hotspot ranking, while each detection still shows what its sensor originally reported. The map changes its representation with zoom, so a week with a quarter of a million detections stays readable worldwide and down to a single pixel. Evaluators can load new data themselves from the interface and watch the job finish.

Factors we considered

- Scientific honesty: a detection is a thermal anomaly, not a confirmed fire, and the interface says so. Near real-time and archive data are kept apart.

- Data limits: FIRMS products have different availability windows, so a job reports clearly when a product has no data for a period.

- Performance: aggregation on the server, indexed queries and chunked inserts keep global views fast.

- Security: the FIRMS key never appears in logs, and secrets stay out of the repository.

- Openness: the code, a user guide and the API reference are public.
